title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — the number-one conversation opener in the Netherlands — name the seasons, and use *er* to say that something exists.
bekal: talking about the weather without running out of things to say
using *er is / er zijn* to say "there is / there are"
wave: Go back to **unit 10**: take ten of your own sentences, move the time expression to the front, and flip the verb.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Lekker weertje
dialogs.intro: Rain, then sun, then rain again — all within an hour. Budi is starting to understand something about this country.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: This morning the sun was still shining.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Ja, en nu regent het weer. Typisch Nederlands.
lines.id: Yes, and now it's raining again. Typically Dutch.
lines.literal: yes, and now rains it again. typically Dutch.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bij ons regent het ook, maar dan uren achter elkaar.
lines.id: It rains where I'm from too, but then for hours on end.
lines.literal: at us rains it also, but then hours behind each-other.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Hier duurt het tien minuten. En dan waait het.
lines.id: Here it lasts ten minutes. And then it gets windy.
lines.literal: here lasts it ten minutes. and then blows it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: De wind is het ergste. Mijn paraplu is al kapot.
lines.id: The wind is the worst. My umbrella is already broken.
lines.literal: the wind is the-worst. my umbrella is already broken.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Daarom gebruikt niemand hier een paraplu. We dragen een regenjas.
lines.id: That's why nobody here uses an umbrella. We wear a raincoat.
lines.literal: that's-why uses nobody here an umbrella. we wear a rain-coat.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En fietsen jullie ook in de regen?
lines.id: And you still cycle in the rain?
lines.literal: and cycle you(pl) also in the rain?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Natuurlijk. Anders kom je nooit ergens.
lines.id: Of course. Otherwise you'd never get anywhere.
lines.literal: naturally. otherwise come you never somewhere.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wordt het nog warm deze zomer?
lines.id: Will it get warm this summer?
lines.literal: becomes it still warm this summer?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Er zijn drie mooie dagen. Meestal in juli.
lines.id: There are three nice days. Usually in July.
lines.literal: there are three nice days. usually in July.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Three days. I'll make a note of it.

notes: **Wat een weer!** — "what weather!". The pattern *wat een + noun* works for any exclamation: *Wat een dag!*, *Wat een mooi huis!*
**Het regent** — weather always takes an empty *het* as its subject, exactly like the *it* in English *it's raining*. Dutch, like English, can't leave it out.
**Typisch Nederlands** — a phrase you'll often hear the Dutch say about their own country, usually half complaining and half proud.
**Uren achter elkaar** = for hours on end. *Achter elkaar* means "one after another", handy for anything in a row.
**Niemand gebruikt een paraplu** — and this is no joke: in a North Sea wind, an umbrella lasts about one season. The Dutch wear a *regenjas* and *regenbroek* (rain pants), and keep pedaling.
**Anders kom je nooit ergens** — *anders* (otherwise), *ergens* (somewhere), *nergens* (nowhere). A group of words that returns in unit 14.

**Wordt het warm?** — *worden* means "to become" and is used for change: *het wordt koud* (it's getting cold), *hij wordt dertig* (he's turning thirty). It's also the verb that forms the passive — an A2 matter.

grammars.title: Weather: sentences with an empty subject
body: Every weather sentence uses *het* as an empty subject, and many are single verbs — Dutch says "it rains", "it blows", "it freezes" where English often needs "it is" + an adjective.
after: Temperature uses *graden* (degrees Celsius): *Het is achttien graden.* Below zero: *Het is min drie* or *drie graden onder nul*.
⚠️ *Het is koud* (the weather is cold) differs from *Ik heb het koud* (I'm cold) — recall unit 4. Mixing them up is a classic beginner's mistake.

grammars.title: Er is / er zijn — there is, there are
body: To say that something not yet mentioned exists, Dutch uses *er* — the equivalent of English *there is/are*.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: **Is er** een supermarkt in de buurt?
In July there are nice days.

after: Look at the last row: once a sentence opens with an adverbial, the second-position rule still applies and *er* moves behind the verb.
*Er* is used for **indefinite** things — *een probleem*, *drie dagen*, *geen koffie*. For something specific, the sentence is ordinary: *De koffie staat op tafel.*
The word *er* has many other jobs in Dutch (you met *ik heb er twee* in unit 2). This is the most common and the easiest — master it first.

blocks.title: Dutch weather in numbers
items: On average **it rains on about 130 days a year** — but almost always briefly. That's why forecasts talk about *buien* (short showers), not "rainy days".
Summers rarely go above 25 °C (77 °F), winters rarely below −5 °C (23 °F). What makes the cold bite is the **wind and humidity**, not the numbers.

*Elfstedentocht* — a 200 km skating race through eleven Frisian towns, held only when every canal freezes thick enough. It last took place in 1997, and every winter the whole country still talks about whether it might happen.
The darkest month is December: the sun rises at 8:30 and sets at 4:30. Many newcomers are shocked by that, not by the temperature.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Volgens het weerbericht gaat het regenen.
The forecast says it's going to rain.
It's not as bad as all that.

blocks.text: *Het valt mee* and *het valt tegen* are a very Dutch pair with no neat English equivalent: the first means "it turned out better than expected", the second "it turned out worse". Used for weather, exams, prices, and almost everything else.

Talking about the weather isn't empty chitchat in the Netherlands — it's a legitimate conversation opener, even with strangers at a bus stop. Two fluent weather sentences will get you further than a paragraph of perfect grammar.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks to complete the weather sentences.
Fill in the blanks with er is or er zijn.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Er is — Er zijn — Er is — Er zijn — Is er
Vandaag regent het. — Het is heel koud. — Ik heb het koud. — Wordt het morgen beter? — Is er een supermarkt in de buurt? — Neem je regenjas mee.
Het regent weer. — Het is vandaag koud. — Er zijn drie mooie dagen. — Neem een paraplu mee. — Wordt het morgen beter?
